title: Ghosts of Lessons Past Pt 3
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien continues his series on lessons he would no longer teach, here targeting the engagement illusion from Instructional Illusions by Heal, Hendrick and Kirschner. He confesses to building units around activities, such as a rumball cook-off and a trade game, that were memorable but taught the wrong lesson or relied on knowledge students lacked. For each he explains what he would change: move them to revision, add checks for understanding, or replace them with whiteboard tasks. His closing model is simple: secure attention, explicitly teach in chunks, check for understanding and re-teach, so that learning itself is the reward rather than gamified points.
points: The engagement illusion: a busy, attentive-looking classroom does not show that students are learning the right thing.
Activities remembered for their novelty can crowd out the curriculum connection, especially when students lack prior knowledge.
Complex simulations suit revision, after foundational knowledge is secure, and need frequent checks for understanding.
A plain loop of attention, chunked explicit teaching, checking and re-teaching builds intrinsic motivation without gamification.
quotes: One of the biggest problems we face in curriculum development is that often we get distracted and build units around activities rather than backwards mapping the knowledge which is most important.
Another example of this could be a classroom where all students are quiet, but their eyes are tracking the teacher and therefore it looks like learning is occurring.

The activity itself, despite being incredibly engaging and memorable was remembered for the activity, not the connection to the curriculum to which it was supposed to be serving. Even worse, some of the curriculum connections were to be made to content they would be learning in future so there was no prior knowledge to actually connect to and therefore they were more likely to learn the wrong lesson which is more difficult to correct later.
Essentially it was an activity which had set the students up to fail because no one had ever given them the tools to approach it optimally.

As I’ve quoted before Greg Ashman has said “knowledge is what you think with” and that has stuck with me ever since. Unless the students have the foundational knowledge, they cannot possibly do the thinking expected of them to succeed and show understanding.

I think a simpler model for engagement and learning is that we follow the following processes. Secure attention, explicitly teach (in chunked form) and check for understanding, then re-teach as necessary.
It feels great to learn something new, so much better than the cheap dopamine hit of flashing lights and a points total.
